80. **No millisecond budget.** Decided on 2026-11-08 at 08:50. There is no millisecond budget. A
   feature is first made to work and to perform well, and its numbers are worked on after or along
   the way as much as possible. So a mend that brings a view to its reference lands by its figures,
   its cost measured and recorded beside them and cut after or along the way where a cut holds the
   readings; item 114 and the rest land or stay by their figures, the cost a figure and not a gate,
   and the forest's and the meadow's milliseconds stay in each record.

81. **A stop rule and one target.** On 2026-11-08 at 08:5x, on the question why the light leaking
   had moved little in days, the direction was that the review does what it thinks right and reports
   it for approval. Approved at 08:49 on 2026-11-08, so a view inside its band lands and a figure
   that remains is recorded and not chased unless it lies in a scene that is looked at, the meadow
   here and Sponza's named views in the engine; one bounded read places a cause and a second is the
   last before a mend is tried or the figure recorded. The meadow at eight in the morning is the
   bridge's one target scene, its crowns and its grass against the one reference, the rooms the
   guard.

83. **Version tags.** Decided at about 14:00 on 2026-11-08, after every commit of the Unity
    Essentials repositories was tagged as `v2.0.30` and the like, the three projects take tags too,
    with the review's questions answered at 14:1x. The form is `v6.0.91`, the letter v before
    `build/version.sh`'s number. Tags go on each major or minor change and on the commits packages
    were built from, since a tag on every commit clutters the list and is unnecessary, the tags
    marking releases some time apart with meaningful changes and not commits apart. The major and
    the minor are the sessions' to raise, each session working on the project deciding when the time
    is right to raise the minor or the major, every commit counting as a patch, with full liberty
    once a step is done and meaningful changes were made. N 6.3 holds the rule and the reviewer sets
    the tags as it pushes. `v0.6.0` marks the commit that set 0.6 and `v0.6.18` the commit
    `b8cc8316` the package of 0.6.18 was published from on 2026-11-02, both set at 14:12.

84. **No middle dot.** Decided at 17:57 and 18:00 on 2026-11-08, the middle dot is not used, the
    README's top links separated by a space alone and the dot nowhere else; the reviewer changed the
    README's first line in the tree on that decision, for the next commit to carry, and every other
    middle dot in the repository is item 118's. The rule goes into STYLE.md's Punctuation as the
    shared text has it everywhere.

85. **One repository, many projects.** The engines' future was thought through with the review at
    about 18:20 on 2026-11-08, after Unity Essentials, where every feature is a repository of its
    own. The points made were that the engines are somewhat cluttered and should be modular,
    extendable, stable and easy to use, that splitting everything into repositories adds clutter and
    makes commits awkward, that the shared modules' repositories are right, that the engine's own
    content could be made modular the same way inside its repository, and that one running process,
    edited and seen as it changes, is worth thinking about; the review's recommendation was approved
    at 18:30. The direction is that each engine stays one repository and becomes one solution of
    many projects, each an area with its own public surface and its own plugin, packed as its own
    package at one version for all, as Bevy's crates are in Bevy's one repository; the dependency
    direction is held by project references and a norm test over them; the flat API stays unchanged
    on top and a game names the packages it needs; the names are dotted .NET names and not com.;
    there is no editor, and the live path is a watcher that recompiles a changed shader, reloads a
    changed asset or scene and recompiles a changed behavior into the running process, the engine's
    own code by restart. It is scheduled after the current items and done as one mechanical batch
    per engine with the public API held identical before and after and the documents' tables
    redrawn. Items 119 and 120, 3DEngine Decision 102.

86. **Comments on the code's own terms.** A comment of scenes_sponza was read at about 19:00 on
    2026-11-08, "The frame graded as that scene's HDRP profile grades it, by the look of its AgX -
    Powerful.exr, a lookup build/unity-lut.py writes from that strip, a gamma of w 0.225, and a
    bloom of intensity 0.25, threshold 0.333 and scatter 0.7, worked out as HDRP works them out",
    and found to read badly, to read as an em dash does, and to lean too far on outside knowledge
    and on the sessions' knowledge of work in progress, in scenes_sponza explicitly and probably
    everywhere else. The rule from it, in STYLE.md's Register and as N 4.11, is that a comment
    stands on the code's own terms. It says what the code does and why in the engine's words; a
    number taken from elsewhere stands with the reason it is right here, what it makes the frame or
    the program do, and the source is named once in the documents' references and not in the
    comment; the file names of outside assets, another product's profile or process as the
    explanation, "as X works it out", and the facts of the sessions' work are not written in a
    comment. Item 121, 3DEngine Decision 103.

87. **No readings or costs in comments.** Decided at about 05:20 on 2026-11-09, on scenes_sponza's
    comment on the far cascade of 100 that carried the lion's end wall's reading from 34.6 to 15.1
    times its reference and the mend's 0.6 ms, a comment need not name the progress or the
    millisecond count, a comment being no protocol. N 4.11 widens so that a comment carries no

146's medium findings 26 to 28, the shader targets' copies, instances that could never be freed and
buffers never forgotten, in the commit carrying this Reply, each with a test that failed without its
mend, and the bridge's ABI at 327.

A value set by name on a material or an instance is written where the target stands, since every
change refuses before it writes, and its layout is read from the program table without copying the
program, where each set copied the whole target with every value it held and the whole program
beside it. A value set again as it stands, a name taken off that has none and a read leave the
target unmarked, so a pass keeps the bind group it built and a material is not prepared again, where
every set marked it. The bridge's test only_a_change_moves_an_instance_on sets one number twice,
another, reads, and takes the name off twice. Without the mend the instance's version went 1, 2, 3,
3, 4 and 5, every set and taking off moving it on, and with it 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 and 3. A pass or a
material whose image is changed in place keeps reading it, since Bevy writes the new texels into the
texture it has, and a buffer grown is bound again as before.

bcs_shader_instance_destroy takes an instance away, its values and the images and buffers they name
with it, through Shaders.DestroyInstance, and its number names nothing after, so a value set on it
or a camera given it is refused and a pass, a draw or a dispatch of it a camera has is left out.
Nothing could take an instance away, so the strong handles in its values kept every image and buffer
it last named for the rest of the app. The rain takes its instances away and lets its buffers go
where it is made again at another quality or taken off, and its roofs' map does the same with its
instance, its images and its camera's target where it is made again over other layers, which each
kept before. Of the places the finding names, the sky's rain is where an instance is dropped within
an app. WorldProbes making its instances again is finding 40, which goes with 138, the clouds' noise
made again for every seed is 41, which waits for a free GPU, and the look keeps each camera's pass
by design, so it is taken off and put back with no compile.
PrecipitationTests.RainMadeAgainLetsGoOfWhatItReplaces makes a camera's rain again four times, at
two qualities over two layers' roofs, and counts the images and shader buffers the app holds after
each. Without the mend the app held 18 images and 11 shader buffers after the first change and 22
and 21 after the third, the same settings again, and with it as many after the third as after the
first, and after the fourth as after the second.

An instance buffer or a material buffer is forgotten once nothing but the bridge holds it, its key
released and no value naming it, and the textures its slots named go with it, where every buffer
ever made stayed and was filled every frame. A ray scene is taken away by Shaders.DestroyRayScene,
through bcs_shader_ray_scene_destroy, and the render world lets go of its structures the next frame,
so GiReference takes away the scene it replaces as its capacity doubles.
ComputeShaderTests.AnInstanceBufferNothingHoldsGoes makes an instance buffer and a material buffer
and releases both. Without the mend the app's shader buffers read 0 before, 2 with both made and 2
once both were released, and with it 0, 2 and 0. SpirvComputeTests.ARaySceneTakenAwayIsGone takes a
scene away and finds it gone to RebuildRayScene, and taking it away again answers false, on a device
with ray queries, and the bridge's a_buffer_nothing_else_holds_is_forgotten holds the forgetting to
the handle's count.

The whole suite over these commits failed ComputeShaderTests.AnInstanceBufferNothingHoldsGoes once,
the memory command's answer reading as NULs after the figures of the managed side. Native.ReadText
asks a writer for the text's length and then for the text, and the memory text grew between the two
while the render thread allocated, so its writer, given too little, wrote nothing and the buffer
came back as it was made. An answer longer than the buffer is asked for again against a buffer of
that length until one fits, eight times at most after the first, and a text longer at each of those
eight asks throws an InvalidOperationException naming what was read, as one growing faster than it
is read, in this commit.
TextConventionTests.TextThatGrowsBetweenCallsIsTruncatedRatherThanOverrunning had its stand-in write
into a buffer too small for its text, which no writer of the bridge does, and it gives way to three.
TextThatGrowsBetweenCallsIsAskedForAgain has a writer keeping the convention whose text grows
between the first call and the second, TextThatShrinksBetweenCallsIsReadAsWritten one whose text
shrinks, and TextLongerAtEveryAskIsAnError one whose text is longer at each of its first twenty
calls. Without the asking again the first read 300 NULs where its writer's text was 900 letters,
without the count the third returned the text of its writer's twenty-first call, and with both the
class's eight passed, and that test of the instance buffers with MemoryCommandTests, the memory
command's readers, passed three runs of three before the count and one after it.

146's medium findings 48 and 49, the Slang module's scratch folder and its search for slangc, in the

The scratch folder is made in a folder of the user's own, the runtime folder the session gives the
user, then the user's cache folder, at 0700, where it was one name in the shared temporary folder
that another account could make first, failing every compile or swapping the modules every shader
imports. Windows and macOS give each account a temporary folder of its own, which it stays in there,
and where neither folder is named it is a new one in the temporary folder made for the process
alone, a name another account took passed over. The bridge's test
the_scratch_folder_is_the_users_own finds it in the user's folder at 0700, and a taken name passed
over. Without the mend it stood in /tmp, and with it in the user's folder.

slangc is looked for in the build/tools of the checkout the program or the working folder is in, the
nearest folder above holding BevyCSharp.slnx, and on Unix only where the user running the program
owns it and no other account can write it, where every folder above was looked in, so a build/tools
another account made at the root of a disk or in a shared temporary folder ran beside any game below
it. The bridge's test only_the_checkouts_own_compiler_is_found plants a compiler above a marked
checkout, then puts one in the checkout and makes it writable by all. Without the mend the planted
one was found, and with it none, the checkout's own, and none once anyone could write it.
Shaders.SlangAvailable says where it is looked for.
